Different people open a groovebox for different reasons. None of these is the
    beginner one. The screen below does not change — only where you are looking.
after: Laser-focused on making music, not learning workflows. Jolt is designed from the ground-up to be mobile-first, inspired by classic handheld devices.

before:
Tap steps until it moves. The Drum Synth is x0x-style — hats, snares and heavy kicks,
          synthesised rather than chosen from a folder.
after: Choose an instrument, and tap in a rhythm or select the steps you want to play.

before: Sixteen steps on screen. Up to sixty-four when the idea needs the room.
after: When your idea needs more space or variation, extend a pattern up to 8 pages of 16 steps.

before:
That kick belongs to the step, not to the voice. Step four of the same lane can be a
            chord, and nothing had to be added to hold it.
after: Mix instruments to make complex grooves - think of instruments as a preset, not a limitation.

before:
Record through the mic, or load an mp3 or a wav. The Sampler plays pitched or sliced, with
          old-skool repitching rather than time-stretching.
after:
Record through the mic, or load a sample in from your library.

Jolt's Sampler features slicing and old-skool repitching, for crafting awesome breaks or remixing classic samples.

before:
Reversing is per step. One slice forward, the same slice backwards on the next step,
            in the same lane.
after: The granular instrument lets you turn any sample into a texture, as sparse or dense as you like.

before:
The Classic Synth is wavetable, with four modes — spread, 2-op FM, paraphony, and
          in-scale chords. The Macro Synth carries sixteen sub-synths built on the architecture of a
          classic Eurorack module.
after:
JOLT's synths cover a wide set of styles, and are all designed for quickly testing out ideas.

Play notes in on the on-screen keyboard, or via MIDI, the load up the piano-roll to edit and tweak until you get the perfect line.

before:
Scale lives in a mode, not over the whole instrument. In-scale chords is one of the
            Classic Synth’s four; the other three are not constrained.
after: Sound editing is as simple as dragging dials and dialling in modulation - no menu diving, and immediately visible.

before:
Generative is one of three ways a step arrives — alongside programming it by hand and
          playing it in over MIDI. All three write to the same lane.
after:
JOLT's generative modes cover simple arpeggios, pounding acid patterns, and a complex chord progression editor.

Everything is kept in-scale, so inspiration is as simple as picking a mode and going wild.

before:
A per-instrument LFO — sine, ramp or random — is freely assignable, so what
            the pattern does and what the sound does need not agree.
after: Most generative modes also allow you to transpose your patterns, to break out of the loop and build up a song.

before: Built on the architecture of a classic Eurorack module.
after: Built on the architecture of the Eurorack classic, Mutable Instruments Plaits.

before: Old-skool repitching, per-step reversing, mic recording, mp3 and wav loading.
after: Old-skool repitching, per-step reversing, and granular cloud.
